answer: Hi, thanks for banking with us! For 2026, the 401(k) employee deferral limit is $24,500. Since you mentioned you're 52, you can add a catch-up contribution of $8,000 on top of that limit, which brings your personal ceiling to $32,500. You told me you plan to contribute $1,500 a month, or $18,000 for the year, so you still have room to raise it.

Good news: the IRA contribution limit is $7,000 this year. Since you're 54, you can also add the IRA catch-up of $1,100 on top of it. You've already put in $3,200 since January, so you could still contribute the difference before the April filing deadline.

Required minimum distributions must begin at age 72. Since you're 67, you have a few years before that kicks in. Be careful once it does: if you miss one, the IRS penalty is 50% of the amount you failed to withdraw, so set up automatic withdrawals from your $640,000 IRA.

Your employer matches 100% of the first 4% of salary you defer. On your $85,000 salary, that works out to $3,400 of matching money each year. If you only defer 2%, you'd leave $1,700 of that match on the table. I'd recommend bumping your deferral to at least 4% at the next payroll cycle.

Here's how your 2026 federal income tax works as a single filer. First, subtract the standard deduction of $16,100 from your $72,000 salary, leaving $55,900 of taxable income. Then apply the brackets:

| Rate | Taxable income |
|---|---|
| 10% | up to $12,400 |
| 12% | up to $50,400 |
| 22% | up to $105,700 |

Your top dollars fall in the 22% bracket, but only the slice above $50,400 is taxed at that rate.

For 2026, the HSA contribution limit for family coverage is $8,550. If you're 55 or older (you mentioned you turn 58 in May), you can add $1,000 to that. Your plan's $4,000 family deductible clears the 2026 HDHP minimum of $3,400, so you're eligible. Your employer seeds $1,200, which counts toward the limit.

Here are the 2026 numbers you asked about:
- 401(k) deferral: $24.5K
- IRA: $7.5K
- HSA (self-only): $4,400
- SIMPLE IRA: $17,000

You said you're saving $500 a month into your Roth IRA. That's $6,000 for the year, comfortably under the IRA cap, so you could add another $125 a month if cash flow allows.

2026 contribution limits:
- 401(k) / 403(b): $23,500
- Catch-up (age 50+): $8,000
- IRA: $7,500

With your current balance of $212,000 and a 6% deferral on $110,000, you're contributing $6,600 a year, well below the first limit above.

The Social Security wage base for 2026 is $180,000. Since your salary is $210,000, you'll stop paying the Social Security portion of payroll tax once your year-to-date wages pass that cap, likely in November. Separately, retirees will see a 2.8% COLA on their benefits this year.

If your $50,000 balance earns an expected 7% a year, the rule of 72 says it doubles roughly every 10 years, so it would be about $100,000 in a decade and $200,000 in two. Real returns will vary, and a 5% assumption would be more conservative. Adding $300 a month would speed that up considerably.

Starting in 2026, employees aged 60 through 63 get a bigger catch-up. You told me you turn 61 this year, so your catch-up isn't the usual $8,000; it's $11,250. Combined with the $24,500 base limit, you can defer up to $35,750 through payroll. Your current election of 15% on $140,000 is $21,000, so there's room to raise it.

HSA limits are going up again. The self-only limit rises from $4,400 in 2026 to $4,500 in 2027, and the family limit goes from $8,750 to $9,000. You're on family coverage and planned to contribute $7,000 this year, so you could add $1,750 more before year end.

The SIMPLE IRA deferral limit is $16,500 for this year. Since you're 57, you can add a catch-up of $3,500 to that limit. Your employer's 3% match on your $60,000 salary adds $1,800, which doesn't count against it.

If you take the $40,000 as a check, your plan has to withhold 20%, so you'd receive $32,000. You then have 90 days to deposit the full $40,000 into an IRA to complete the rollover, using other savings to cover the $8,000 that was withheld. Anything you don't roll over could also face the 10% early-distribution tax since you're 52.

In 2026 you can give each person up to $19,000 without filing a gift tax return. You plan to give your three grandchildren $15,000 each, which is under the exclusion. If your spouse agrees to split gifts, the two of you could give up to $38,000 per grandchild.

The annual gift tax exclusion is $18,000 for this year. Since you want to give your daughter $20,000 toward her down payment, you'd exceed that amount by $2,000 and would need to file Form 709, though you almost certainly won't owe any tax.

If you claim Social Security before full retirement age, there's an annual earnings limit, which is $23,400 for 2026. Since you're 64 and expect to earn $30,000 from consulting, you'd be over it by $6,600, and some of your benefits would be withheld until you reach FRA.

Your benefit will get the 2026 COLA of 2.8%, so your $2,100 monthly payment rises to about $2,159. For context, the maximum benefit at full retirement age in 2026 is $4,152 a month, so you're about half of it.

The maximum Social Security benefit at full retirement age is $4,500 per month in 2026. To get it you'd need 35 years of earnings at or above the taxable maximum, which is $184,500 this year. Your statement shows a projected $3,050, which is quite strong.

Your Premier Savings account currently earns 4.10% APY on your $12,350 balance. If you move $10,000 into our 9-month CD at 4.35%, you'd earn about $326 over the term. Early withdrawal from the CD carries a 90-day interest penalty.

RMDs start at age 73. Since you turned 73 in March, your first RMD is due by April 1 of next year, though taking it this year avoids doubling up. Your custodian estimates it at $18,100. If you miss it, the excise tax is 25% of the shortfall, reduced to 10% if you correct it within 2 years.

The HSA limit for self-only coverage is $4,300 for 2026. Because you're 56, you can add $1,000 on top of that limit. You've contributed $2,000 so far and your employer puts in $750, which counts toward it too, so plan your remaining contributions accordingly.

Withdrawing $25,000 from your 401(k) now, at 52, would trigger a 15% additional tax for early distribution, on top of ordinary income tax. The plan will also withhold 20% up front, so you'd net about $20,000 before settling the rest at tax time.

Here are the 2026 standard deductions:

| Filing status | Standard deduction |
|---|---|
| Single | $16,100 |
| Married filing jointly | $32,200 |
| Head of household | $24,150 |

You estimated $28,000 of itemized deductions (mortgage interest plus state taxes). Since you file jointly, the standard deduction is larger, so you should take it.

For 2026, the standard deduction is $16,100 for single filers and $31,500 for married couples filing jointly. Since you and your wife have $27,000 in itemizable expenses, the standard deduction still wins.

Open enrollment runs November 3 through November 21. If you pick the HDHP, the company contributes $600 to your HSA, and your premium drops to $142 per paycheck from $198. Over 26 paychecks that's $1,456 in savings.

The Social Security taxable maximum is $176,100 this year, so on your $195,000 salary you'll stop seeing Social Security tax withheld once you pass it, around your November paycheck. Medicare tax continues on every dollar.

For 2026 you can defer up to 24.5 thousand dollars into your 403(b), and the IRA limit is 7.5 thousand. Your employer's 4% match on your $90,000 salary is $3,600 and doesn't reduce what you can defer.
The 2026 IRA limit is $7,500, and the IRA catch-up for savers 50 and older is $1,500, so at 59 you could contribute up to $9,000 in total. You've put in $4,000 so far.

Yes, you can contribute to both plans. The 457(b) limit (same as the 401(k) limit, $23,500 for 2026) applies separately from your 401(k), and you can add the catch-up ($8,000 if you're 50 or older) to each. With your $165,000 salary, maxing both is realistic.

Since you're 67 and still working, you can keep contributing to the TSP: the 2026 limit is $24,500 plus the $8,000 catch-up. Your traditional IRA is different, though: RMDs from it begin at 73, so you have a few years. Your TSP balance of $520,000 isn't subject to RMDs while you remain employed by the agency.
The earnings limit rises from $23,400 in 2026 to $24,480 in 2027. You're 63 and expect $26,000 in part-time wages next year, so you'd be just over it.
You need to start RMDs at age 70½, and since you're already 71, you're behind. Take the distribution from your $300,000 IRA as soon as possible to limit the penalty.
To be HSA-eligible in 2026, your plan's deductible must be at least $1,650 for self-only coverage or $3,400 for family coverage. Your plan's $2,500 single deductible qualifies.

For 2026 the SIMPLE IRA limit is $17,000. Because you're 51, you can add $4,000 on top of it. Your employer matches 3% of your $70,000 salary, which is $2,100, and that match doesn't count against it.

A simple budgeting starting point is the 50/30/20 rule: 50% for needs, 30% for wants, 20% for savings. On your $5,200 monthly take-home, that's $2,600, $1,560, and $1,040. Since your rent is $2,100, needs may run higher, so trim wants first.
This year's COLA was 2.5%, so your $1,850 benefit went up by about $46. If you go back to work before full retirement age, remember the 2026 earnings limit of $24,480.
The 401(k) limit went from $23.5K in 2025 to $24.5K in 2026, and the catch-up went from $7.5K to $8K. Your planned $20K this year leaves you $4.5K of room under the new limit.
Your family HSA limit for 2026 is $8,750. The HSA catch-up is $2,000 once you hit 55, and since you're 56 you qualify. Your $6,500 planned contribution leaves room for more.

On the refinance: your $310,000 balance at 6.25% vs. a new rate of 5.6% saves about $135 a month. On your other question, the 2026 IRA limit is $7,500, so the $5,000 you planned to put in this year is fine, and it has no effect on the mortgage.
